Case 5:24-cv-04793-PCP           Document 51       Filed 06/02/26      Page 1 of 5




                                   1

                                   2

                                   4                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                 NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7     RADUS TEK SERVICES, INC.,                         Case No. 24-cv-04793-PCP
                                                        Plaintiff,
                                   8
                                                                                           ORDER GRANTING MOTION FOR
                                                 v.                                        DEFAULT JUDGMENT
                                   9

                                  10     IDC TECHNOLOGIES INC., et al.,                    Re: Dkt. No. 49
                                                        Defendants.
                                  11

                                  12          Plaintiff Radus Tek Services, Inc. (Radus Tek) moves for entry of default judgment against
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   defendants IDC Technologies (IDC) and Prateek Gattani. Radus Tek alleges that, pursuant to a

                                  14   contract with IDC, it provided defendants with the service of two information technology staffers,

                                  15   for which Radus Tek was to be compensated at the end of each month. IDC, however, failed to

                                  16   pay fourteen Radus Tek invoices totaling $144,704.00. Gattani is the “majority shareholder, the

                                  17   only Director, the Chief Operating Officer, the Secretary and the Chief Financial Officer for IDC

                                  18   Technologies.”

                                  19          Radus Tek sued IDC, Gattani, and Tata Consultancy Services on August 7, 2024. Radus

                                  20   Tek effected service on IDC and Gattani on October 2, 2024. After this Court granted Tata

                                  21   Consultancy Services’ motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim under Federal Rule of Civil

                                  22   Procedure 12(b)(6), Radus Tek voluntarily dismissed its case against Tata Consultancy Services

                                  23   without prejudice on June 9, 2025, leaving only IDC and Gattani in this litigation.

                                  24          After voluntarily dismissing Tata Consultancy Services, Radus Tek moved for entry of

                                  25   default against IDC and Gattani, which the Clerk of Court entered on June 30, 2025. On

                                  26   November 6, 2025, Radus Tek filed the instant motion for entry of default judgment. The Court

                                  27   heard argument on the motion from Radus Tek. At no point in these proceedings has IDC or

                                  28   Gattani made an appearance.
                                         Case 5:24-cv-04793-PCP            Document 51         Filed 06/02/26     Page 2 of 5




                                   1   I.      Default Judgment

                                   2           Federal Rule 55(b)(2) allows a party “to apply to the court for a default judgment.” The

                                   3   decision to enter a default judgment is entirely within the district court's discretion. Aldabe v.

                                   4   Aldabe, 616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980). Courts consider the following factors in determining

                                   5   whether default judgment is proper:

                                   6                  (1) the possibility of prejudice to the plaintiff, (2) the merits of
                                   7                  plaintiff’s substantive claim, (3) the sufficiency of the complaint,
                                                      (4) the sum of money at stake in the action; (5) the possibility of a
                                   8                  dispute concerning material facts; (6) whether the default was due to
                                                      excusable neglect, and (7) the strong policy underlying the Federal
                                   9                  Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on the merits.
                                  10   Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471–72 (9th Cir. 1986). Where a plaintiff seeks default against a
                                  11   non-appearing defendant, the court “should determine whether it has the power, i.e., the
                                  12   jurisdiction, to enter the judgment in the first place.” In re Tuli, 172 F.3d 707, 712 (9th Cir. 1999).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   The Court must also assess the adequacy of service of process on the non-appearing party. See,
                                  14   e.g., Innovative Sports Management, Inc. v. Nunez, No. 22-cv-07136-JSC, 2023 WL 4551069, at
                                  15   *2 (N.D. Cal. July 13, 2023).
                                  16           The Eitel factors supporting entering default judgment against the defendants. The first
                                  17   Eitel factor supports default judgment because without default judgment Radus Tek will be unable
                                  18   to legally obtain compensation for the services it provided IDC. The second and third Eitel factors
                                  19   support default judgment because Radus Tek’s complaint states a facially valid cause of action
                                  20   against IDC for breach of contract. The fourth factor favors default judgment because the sum of
                                  21   money at stake reflects the services Radus Tek provided to IDC without compensation. The fifth
                                  22   factor is neutral because the Court cannot know whether there will be a dispute concerning
                                  23   material facts given that defendants have not appeared in this action. The sixth factor favors
                                  24   default judgment because defendants were served and have not appeared nor does there appear to
                                  25   be a justifiable reason for default. The seventh factor, “the strong policy underlying the Federal
                                  26   Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on the merits,” weighs against default judgment
                                  27   because of the Federal Rules’ “strong policy” of deciding cases on the merits. Eitel, 782 F.2d at
                                  28   1472.
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 5:24-cv-04793-PCP            Document 51          Filed 06/02/26     Page 3 of 5




                                   1          Thus, the first, second, third, fourth, and sixth factors favor entry of default judgment, the

                                   2   fifth is neutral, and the seventh weighs against its entry. Because “numerous factors weigh in favor

                                   3   of entry of default judgment,” Radus Tek’s motion for entry of default judgment is granted. See

                                   4   NewGen, 840 F.3d at 616.

                                   5   II.    Damages

                                   6          Radus Tek requests actual damages, prejudgment interest, fees, costs, and postjudgment

                                   7   interest. The Court considers each in turn.

                                   8          First, Radus Tek requests contractual damages for the services provided by Radus Tek

                                   9   employees Syed Muhammed Raheel Hassan and Firoz Makati. Radus Tek’s first amended

                                  10   complaint attached invoices from Hassan and Makati showing that they provided $144,704.00 in

                                  11   services to IDC pursuant to the parties’ contract. Those amounts have been further confirmed by a

                                  12   declaration from Radus Tek’s counsel. See NewGen, LLC v. Safe Cig, LLC, 840 F.3d 606, 617
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   (9th Cir. 2016). Radus Tek’s request for $144,704.00 in actual contract damages is adequately

                                  14   supported and therefore granted.

                                  15          Second, Radus Tek requests prejudgment interest on the $144,704.00 balance it is owed

                                  16   dating from the date payment was due to the date of this judgment. California Civil Code Section

                                  17   3287(a) states that “[a] person who is entitled to recover damages certain, or capable of being

                                  18   made certain by calculation, and the right to recover which is vested in the person upon a

                                  19   particular day, is entitled also to recover interest thereon from that day….” California Civil Code

                                  20   Section 3289(b) provides, “If a contract entered into after January 1, 1986, does not stipulate a

                                  21   legal rate of interest, the obligation shall bear interest at a rate of 10 percent per annum after a

                                  22   breach.” The “Professional Services Agreement” that Radus Tek and IDC entered into does not

                                  23   specify a rate of interest for damages stemming from a breach. See Dkt. No. 13, Exhibit B. The

                                  24   Court therefore applies the 10 percent annual interest rate.

                                  25          Radus Tek has calculated the prejudgment interest due for each unpaid invoice based on

                                  26   the number of days that those invoiced amounts are overdue. Radus Tek has calculated the interest

                                  27   that has accrued based on a 10 percent annual interest rate with no compounding from the date an

                                  28   invoice was due to October 28, 2025. Id. Radus Tek also requests prejudgment interest for the
                                                                                           3
                                            Case 5:24-cv-04793-PCP        Document 51        Filed 06/02/26      Page 4 of 5




                                   1   period from October 29, 2025, to the date of this entry of judgment at a rate of $39.64 per day. 1

                                   2   The Court agrees that Radus Tek is entitled to prejudgment interest of $37,459.57 and concludes

                                   3   that Radus Tek’s calculations—of the total prejudgment interest due until October 28, 2025, of

                                   4   $28,857.69, and of the prejudgment interest due from October 29, 2025 to the date of the entry of

                                   5   this judgment—are accurate. The Court therefore grants Radus Tek’s request for prejudgment

                                   6   interest in the amount of $37,459.57.

                                   7           Third, Radus Tek requests attorneys’ fees. Radus Tek’s agreement with IDC provided for

                                   8   the prevailing party to “be entitled to reasonable attorney fees and costs….” Counsel for Radus

                                   9   Tek has declared under penalty of perjury that he expended 78.0 hours of work at a rate of $350

                                  10   per hour, resulting in a $27,300.00 lodestar. Some of counsel’s work was spent litigating Radus

                                  11   Tek’s claims against Tata Consultancy Services, however, and that time is not compensable here.

                                  12   Radus Tek has accordingly requested only $15,000.00. The Court concludes that counsel’s request
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   is reasonable and grants it.

                                  14           Fourth, Radus Tek requests reimbursement of costs incurred in filing this case and

                                  15   engaging the services of a private process-server who had to attempt services multiple times.

                                  16   Radus Tek requests $912.25—$405.00 for the filing fee and $507.25 for process-server fees.

                                  17   Radus Tek’s request is granted.

                                  18           Finally, Radus Tek requests post-judgment interest. Section 1961 of Title 28 of the U.S.

                                  19   Code provides for interest on money judgments in civil cases. 28 U.S.C. § 1961(a). “Such interest

                                  20   shall be calculated from the date of the entry of the judgment, at a rate equal to the weekly average

                                  21   1-year constant maturity Treasury yield, as published by the Board of Governors of the Federal

                                  22   Reserve System, for the calendar week preceding the date of the judgment.” Id. That interest rate

                                  23   is 3.80 percent. See Selected Interest Rates Instruments, Yield in Percent Per Annum, Weekly,

                                  24   Fed. Rsrv. Bank of St. Louis, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?rid=18&eid=290&od=.

                                  25   Radus Tek’s request for post judgment interest is granted.

                                  26
                                       1
                                  27     Radus Tek appears to have calculated the daily prejudgment interest rate by dividing the interest
                                       rate of 10 percent by 365 to get the daily interest rate and then calculating it to the total
                                  28   outstanding amount, $144,704.00. Ten percent divided by 365 multiplied by $144,704.00 equals
                                       $39.64.
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:24-cv-04793-PCP         Document 51        Filed 06/02/26    Page 5 of 5




                                   1          Accordingly, default judgment is entered as to IDC Technologies, Inc., and Prateek Gattani

                                   2   in the amount of $198,075.82, with the amount to increase based on the amount of post-judgment

                                   3   interest due.

                                   4

                                   5          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                   6   Dated: June 2, 2026

                                   7

                                   8
                                                                                                 P. Casey Pitts
                                   9                                                             United States District Judge
